The meek inherit nothing.

God in his tattered coat

Little lamb, paupered flock,

fleece, worn vast spools

The gentle are left with no inheritance.

This morning, God appears in a ragged overcoat,  
murmuring softly beside me, asking for charity,  
his chilled fingers sliding beneath my dress.  
Poor little sheep, destitute congregation,  
season my dark tea with your weeping.

I stripped away your shining wool  
and clothed myself in endless coils  
of ivory lace, luminous brocade,  
golden leaves, and gemstone powder.  
Threads of corn-colored hair line my seams.

I have drained the heavy animal  
you name America,  
and draped its men over my breasts like pelts:  
a fox pinned at the throat, a pale-blue chinchilla.  
They also arrived to feed at my threshold,  
caught in the tender rose-colored knots  
I set for them.

Beloved observers concealed by darkness,  
beloved demons with powerful thighs,  
stand easy.  
Tell the dogs peeling away my clothes with their gaze  
that I conceal nothing.  
I will open my body completely.

Look: muscle gleaming.  
Look: blood spilled for the chase.  
And now, the axis of existence—  
my radiant sex.

Praise the shadowed flowering of amaryllis  
and the untamed blush of Damascus rose,  
my cherished Aphrodite revealing herself  
inside the twist.

Praise jasmine burning after sunset;  
dense sweetness coating your mouth,  
a divided blade resting on my speech.  
Armies follow behind me.

At this crimson holy place of the earth,  
bow down.  
Here is paradise; here is Bethlehem;  
here, within Thebes’s birthplace,  
an immense sphinx prowls among the plants,  
consuming the drenched light of morning.
outputs.L3:
The speaker rejects traditional expectations of feminine meekness, presenting power not as something passively inherited or graciously bestowed, but as something actively seized. She constructs her authority by claiming to have used wealth, luxury, America, and men for her own purposes. Rather than allowing these forces to define or possess her, she appropriates them to create an opulent, commanding identity built on excess, spectacle, and self-invention.

Her unapologetic display of her body is central to this assertion of power. Although she is conscious of the objectifying gaze directed at her, she refuses to remain merely its passive object. Instead, she turns visibility into defiance, using her sexuality to command attention and control how she is perceived. Religious, mythological, and floral imagery further elevates the female body and feminine desire, presenting sexuality as simultaneously sacred, beautiful, dangerous, and worthy of worship. These images transform the speaker from an object of desire into an almost divine or mythic figure.

The poem ultimately culminates in a demand for submission. By insisting that others recognize and yield to her power, the speaker overturns conventional hierarchies in which women are expected to be obedient or restrained. Feminine sexuality is no longer marginal, shameful, or controlled by others; instead, it becomes the central force around which the speaker’s world—and, symbolically, the wider world—must revolve.
outputs.L4:
The poem confronts exploitation, poverty, sexual objectification, and American excess through the voice of a defiant female speaker. Rather than presenting herself as a passive victim, the speaker exposes the economic and social forces that reduce women—and especially poor women—to bodies that can be consumed, judged, or discarded. Her perspective reveals a world in which wealth exists beside deprivation and pleasure depends upon unequal power. Against this landscape of excess, her body becomes both the site of oppression and the instrument through which she resists it.

Religious and mythic imagery allow the speaker to challenge the values imposed upon her. Language traditionally associated with holiness, worship, and creation is redirected toward the female body and its desires. This transformation rejects moral systems that treat female sexuality as sinful or shameful. Instead of seeking purity through denial, the speaker constructs a sacred identity grounded in physical experience, survival, and self-possession. She refuses to accept that spiritual authority belongs only to distant gods, patriarchal institutions, or those protected by wealth.

Animal and erotic imagery further intensify this reversal of power. Images that might ordinarily be used to portray women as primitive, vulnerable, or available are reclaimed as signs of instinct, vitality, and strength. The speaker does not deny that she has been watched or sexualized; instead, she seizes control of the gaze. She presents herself on her own terms, turning exposure into confrontation and desire into a source of agency. Those who look at her are no longer secure in the role of spectators, because her voice makes them visible as participants in the systems she condemns.

The poem’s critique therefore operates on both personal and political levels. The speaker’s assertion of bodily autonomy becomes a challenge to a culture shaped by consumption, inequality, and hypocrisy. American abundance appears grotesque when placed beside hunger and exploitation, while conventional ideas of respectability are revealed as tools for policing women without addressing the conditions that endanger them. The speaker’s erotic confidence resists this hypocrisy by insisting that poverty does not erase dignity and that sexual desire does not eliminate a woman’s right to define herself.

Ultimately, the speaker transforms her sexualized body into a sacred and powerful center of the world. What others have treated as an object becomes a source of meaning, creation, and judgment. By combining the holy with the erotic, the human with the animal, and vulnerability with defiance, she overturns the expectations of shame and submission. The poem thus presents feminine desire and agency not as forces that must be controlled, but as forms of power worthy of recognition and reverence.
outputs.L5:
### The Little God

In a quiet village between the mountains and the sea, people spoke of a little god who lived beneath an ancient oak tree. Unlike the powerful gods of storms and war, he ruled over small things: lost buttons, warm bread, secret smiles, and the courage to begin again.

No one built temples for him. Instead, they honored him whenever they helped a stranger, forgave a mistake, or noticed beauty in an ordinary day.

The little god asked for no praise. He only reminded people that even the smallest act of kindness could change the world.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a provocative free-verse poem in the voice of a wealthy, sexually empowered woman who mocks religion, capitalism, and the male gaze through imagery of luxury, animals, mythology, and the female body.
counterfactuals.output:
**HERETIC IN SILK**

I wake beneath a chandelier  
fat with counterfeit stars,  
each crystal paid for  
by a man who mistook desire  
for ownership.

My sheets are the color of fresh milk.  
My body, the cat at the saucer—  
unhurried, sovereign,  
licking the moon from its paw.

In the chapel of my dressing room  
I keep no saints,  
only mirrors.

I kneel to fasten a diamond at my ankle  
and rise absolved.

God, they told me, was a father.  
Of course.  
Who else would build a world  
and leave the cleaning to women?

I wear Eve’s old hunger  
like couture:  
fig leaves stitched in gold thread,  
the serpent coiled at my throat  
with emerald eyes.

Let the priests choke  
on their incense.  
Let the bankers count  
the ribs of the poor  
as if poverty were a rosary.

I have seen capitalism naked—  
a pink, sweating emperor  
asking whether the yacht  
makes him look immortal.

Darling, nothing does.

At dinner I order oysters,  
pomegranate, the heart  
of a metaphor still beating.

Men look.

Men always look,  
their pupils small black coins  
thrown toward the fountain  
of my breasts, my hips,  
my unpurchased mouth.

They call it admiration  
when they mean appetite.  
They call me cruel  
when the feast looks back.

I am not your Venus  
unless Venus keeps the island,  
the shipping rights,  
the museum gift shop.

I am not your muse.  
I own the gallery.

Watch me cross the marble floor  
in heels sharp enough  
to puncture a stock exchange.

My laughter sends white horses  
bolting through boardrooms.  
My perfume makes wolves  
forget the hunt  
and beg to be brushed.

Somewhere, a golden bull  
lowers his jeweled head.  
Somewhere, Zeus arrives  
disguised as weather.

I close the window.

No gods enter  
without an appointment.

Tonight I bathe in black champagne,  
pearls drifting around me  
like obedient planets.

I raise one wet hand—  
not in prayer,  
not in surrender—

but to toast the beautiful ruin  
of every altar, market, and gaze  
that priced me  
before learning

I was the auction house,  
the fire,  
and the woman  
walking away  
in sable  
with the matches.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a dark feminist poem that begins with “The meek inherit nothing” and transforms a woman’s sexuality into a sacred center of power, blending biblical references with Aphrodite, Thebes, Eden, and the sphinx.
counterfactuals.output:
The meek inherit nothing  
but the dust beneath another’s throne.  
So I rose, ribless, from my own red clay,  
no Adam’s wound, no borrowed bone.

I named my hunger holy.

Between my thighs, a temple burned—  
not altar for the laws of men,  
but oracle, abyss, and genesis,  
the dark amen before amen.

Aphrodite climbed from blackened foam  
with salt and blood upon her mouth;  
she crowned me where they cursed me,  
turned their north toward my south.

Eden withered at my footsteps.  
The serpent whispered, *Take and know.*  
I bit the fruit down to its seeds  
and felt a second heaven grow.

At Thebes I met the sphinx at dusk,  
her lion-haunches slick with rain.  
She asked what walks on wounded feet  
and learns to make a throne of pain.

“Woman,” I said, “when she remembers  
every gate was once her name.”  
The sphinx bowed low. The city shook.  
Its kings went blind inside their shame.

Now scripture smolders in my hands;  
I write new psalms in my own skin.  
My pleasure is no fall from grace—  
it is the place where gods begin.

Let patriarchs nail stars to crosses,  
call desire the devil’s art.  
I keep the sacred center turning:  
womb and mouth and ravenous heart.

No meekness. No inherited earth.  
I claim the root, the grave, the sky.  
I am the question at the threshold.  
I am the answer kings deny.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.output:

Come closer, darling. The chandeliers have begun to molt their diamonds, and the night is already on its knees.

Do you like my dress? Lace pale as a widow’s breath, jacquard woven with pomegranates and little golden knives. At my throat, an emerald sleeps in its nest of pearls; across my shoulders, the fur of some magnificent predator remembers the forest—and trembles because it recognizes me.

I have perfumed the room with tuberose, that indecent flower, and with roses so dark they seem bruised by invisible mouths. Even the orchids are watching us. Look how they open: slow, carnivorous stars.

You should have fled when my carriage arrived.

Instead, you offered me your hand, poor beautiful animal, as though I were a lady stepping over a puddle and not a tigress crossing the last narrow bridge between appetite and possession. I felt your pulse beneath your glove. Such a frantic little bird. Such confidence in its cage.

They say I ruin men. How vulgar. I merely reveal them. Beneath every medal, every oath, every immaculate collar, there is a garden at midnight—wet leaves, crushed violets, serpents gleaming among the lilies. I enter with my jeweled shears. I prune. I harvest. I leave nothing untouched.

Pour the wine. No, from my glass. Let the garnet stain your mouth like evidence.

Tonight the moon has drowned in the fountain, the mirrors have forgotten which of us is real, and my pearls are slipping loose one by one, small pale planets abandoning their orbit. Soon there will be only silk on the floor, flowers gasping in their vases, and your name torn open between my teeth.

Bolt the door.

Come willingly—or let me enjoy the chase.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a contemporary confessional poem about female dominance and excess in America, contrasting beggars and poverty with opulent fashion. Make the language decadent, blasphemous, mythic, and confrontational.
counterfactuals.output:
**AMERICAN GODDESS IN A WINDOW DISPLAY**

I confess: I wanted the whole republic kneeling—  
its bald eagles hooded, its fathers on leashes,  
its dollar bills damp with my lipstick.  
I wanted to enter the party like weather,  
Versace thunder at my hips,  
a little apocalypse stitched into every seam.

Outside, a woman cups January in both hands.  
She asks for change beneath the boutique awning  
where mannequins stare past her in six-thousand-dollar grief.  
Her cardboard sign buckles in the sleet.  
Mine says **LIMITED EDITION**, embossed in gold.  
Tell me which of us America calls holy.

I have eaten grapes from the mouth of power.  
I have worn a white fur coat  
soft as the lie of salvation.  
In the restroom mirror, I crown myself  
with fluorescent light and cocaine snow,  
Madonna of the maxed-out card,  
Aphrodite born from an oil spill.

Men offer me kingdoms:  
corner offices, black cars, their passwords,  
their tender little empires of shame.  
I step on their neckties in crystal heels  
and call it progress.  
They moan like markets opening.  
They thank me for the recession.

But I know the arithmetic.  
One purse equals six months’ rent.  
One gala chandelier burns brighter  
than a block of condemned apartments.  
At dinner, we photograph the truffles  
while a child on the train  
licks salt from a paper sleeve.

O Christ of the velvet rope, forgive me—  
no, don’t.  
I am tired of forgiveness laundering the blood.  
I have seen your body sold in every window:  
thin, jeweled, impossible,  
posed above the beggar like a threat.

So I confess because confession is another luxury:  
I love the silk. I love command.  
I love making the powerful lower their eyes.  
I love the click of my heels  
like a firing squad in a marble lobby.  
I love being feared more than being good.

America, look at me.

I am your favorite daughter,  
your dominatrix in couture,  
your famine wearing diamonds,  
your Liberty with one breast bare  
and one hand rifling the poor box.

Kneel, if you must—  
but open your wallet while you’re down there.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a single-stanza prose poem in which a glamorous woman addresses lustful onlookers, reclaims the male gaze, and commands them to kneel before her body as though it were simultaneously Mecca, Bethlehem, Eden, and an ancient temple.
counterfactuals.output: Look all you like, darlings; I have taken your gaze from you and set it among my jewels, another bright thing made to serve me. You thought desire was an arrow, but in my hands it becomes a crown. I cross the room in silk and thunder, and every hungry eye follows like a pilgrim’s lamp. Kneel—not because I am yours, but because your wanting has arrived at its holy geography: my body, Mecca of your turning, Bethlehem of your astonishment, Eden with the gate flung wide, an ancient temple whose columns remember queens. Bring no conquest here. Bring reverence. Lay down your swagger with your shoes, hush your clever mouths, and learn that beauty is not a country you may enter, but a sovereign before whom you may only tremble, praise, and wait.
